title: Go, Yield, Step Back
theme: The roots ced and cess: going, yielding and stopping
objectives: I can explain that the root ced/cess means go or yield and name three prefixes that change it.
I can use a prefix and the root to work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word.
I can spell words that end in -cede, -ceed, and -cess correctly.
I can write about a conflict using words that describe going, stepping in, and stepping back.
rationale: The Latin root ced/cess, meaning to go or to yield, appears in civics (secede, concession, intercede), economics (recession, excessive), and everyday life (procedure, accessible). Because one root meets many prefixes, students can see how pre-, pro-, re-, se-, inter-, suc-, ac-, and ex- steer the same idea of going in different directions: before, forward, back, apart, between, next, toward, and out. The unit also shows why spelling varies (ced, cede, ceed, cess) and uses one narrative about a town in a dispute so that students see the words together. The unit reaches back to concession, contend, and unilateral from the argument and number-prefix units.

words.def: To come before something in time, order, or position.
words.ex: In the alphabet, the letter B precedes the letter C.
words.ex2: A short welcome will precede each speech, giving the audience some background.
words.nonExample: A runner who finishes after you does not precede you.

morph.note: The root ced becomes cede at the end of this word.

apps.academic: Events that precede a war, such as shortages and disputes, help historians explain its causes.
apps.spoken: Dinner precedes dessert, so eat your vegetables.
apps.writing: Use precede to show order in time, and follow when you want to show what came next.

cloze.s: The lightning flash ___ the thunder by several seconds, which is why you see it first.

cloze2.s: A short introduction will ___ each speech, giving the audience background before the main talk begins.

misuse.s: In a line, the person who precedes you is standing behind you.
misuse.why: To precede is to come before, so the person ahead of you precedes you.

visual.alt: One runner a step ahead of another.

words.def: To go forward or continue, especially after stopping.
words.ex: After the fire drill, the class proceeded to the gym for the assembly.
words.ex2: Please proceed to the next question when you are ready.
words.nonExample: Standing still and refusing to move on is not proceeding.

morph.note: The root ced becomes ceed in this word.

apps.academic: In the experiment, students proceed to the next step only after recording the result.
apps.spoken: May I proceed with my presentation now?
apps.writing: Use proceed to show that an action continues, as in proceeded to explain.

cloze.s: After the long delay, the pilot was cleared to ___ down the runway for takeoff.

cloze2.s: The judge told the lawyer to ___ with her next question.

misuse.s: The class proceeded to stop moving and stay in exactly the same place all day.
misuse.why: To proceed is to go forward; staying in one place is the opposite.

visual.alt: A walking figure beside an arrow pointing forward.

words.def: To move back or away, or to become smaller or weaker.
words.ex: As the floodwater receded, the families could finally return to their street.
words.ex2: The sound of the siren receded as the ambulance drove away.
words.nonExample: A tide rushing higher up the beach is not receding.

morph.note: The root ced becomes cede at the end of this word.

apps.academic: As glaciers recede, they leave behind rocks and valleys that scientists can study.
apps.spoken: The pain finally began to recede.
apps.writing: Use recede for something that moves back or fades, such as water, sound, or fear.

cloze.s: When the tide began to ___, the beach filled with shells and sea glass.

cloze2.s: As the storm moved away, the thunder seemed to ___ into a distant mumble.

misuse.s: The floodwaters receded by rising higher and covering the whole street.
misuse.why: To recede is to move back; rising higher is the opposite.

visual.alt: A wave sliding back from a sandy beach.

words.def: To formally withdraw from a group, organization, or country.
words.ex: In the story, the island's northern villages voted to secede and form their own council.
words.ex2: Several states seceded from the United States in 1860 and 1861.
words.nonExample: Joining a club is not seceding from it.

morph.note: The root ced becomes cede at the end of this word.

apps.academic: In history, a region that secedes declares that it will no longer be part of a larger nation.
apps.spoken: He threatened to secede from the group chat.
apps.writing: Use secede for a formal, official withdrawal, not for simply leaving a room.

cloze.s: The neighborhood threatened to ___ from the city and form its own town if taxes rose again.

cloze2.s: Members of the club voted to ___ and start their own team after the argument over uniforms.

misuse.s: The town seceded by merging even more closely with the larger city.
misuse.why: To secede is to withdraw; merging more closely is the opposite.

visual.alt: Scissors cutting a section away from a map.

words.def: To step in on behalf of someone, especially to help settle a disagreement.
words.ex: The coach interceded when two players started shouting at each other.
words.ex2: Grandma interceded with Dad so that Mia could go on the class trip.
words.nonExample: Walking away from an argument and ignoring it is not interceding.

morph.note: The root ced becomes cede at the end of this word.

apps.academic: A diplomat may intercede with a government to help a citizen who is in trouble.
apps.spoken: Can you intercede for me with the teacher?
apps.writing: Use intercede when someone steps in between two sides or speaks up for another person.

cloze.s: When the argument got heated, the teacher decided to ___ before anyone said something they would regret.

cloze2.s: The mayor agreed to ___ on behalf of the neighbors who had been left without power for three days.

misuse.s: She interceded by walking away and refusing to get involved in any way.
misuse.why: To intercede is to step in between; refusing to get involved is the opposite.

words.def: A period when business slows, people lose jobs, and families spend less money.
words.ex: During the recession, many families cut back on restaurants and trips.
words.ex2: Economists said that the recession would end once businesses began hiring again.
words.nonExample: A time when new stores open and jobs are plentiful is not a recession.
words.rel: a going back of the economy

apps.academic: In a recession, businesses sell less, so some lay off workers.
apps.spoken: My aunt lost her job during the recession.
apps.writing: Use recession for a time of economic decline, not for any bad week.

cloze.s: When a ___ hit the town, stores closed and many workers lost their jobs.

cloze2.s: The government lowered interest rates, hoping to shorten the ___ and help people find work again.

misuse.s: During the recession, businesses hired thousands of new workers and everyone spent more money.
misuse.why: A recession is a time of slowing business and job loss, so growth and more spending are the opposite.

visual.alt: A falling line graph next to a store.

words.frame: During a recession, people may ___ because ___.

words.def: The set of steps followed to do something in a fixed way.
words.ex: The school's fire-drill procedure tells every class which door to use and where to meet.
words.ex2: The nurse followed the same procedure each time she checked the equipment.
words.nonExample: A single random action with no order is not a procedure.

apps.academic: A lab procedure lists the steps so that anyone can repeat the experiment.
apps.spoken: What's the procedure for turning in late work?
apps.writing: Describe a procedure with numbered or time-order steps.

cloze.s: The ___ for borrowing a book is simple: scan your card, scan the book, and wait for the beep.

cloze2.s: Following the lab ___ exactly, the students added the chemicals in the right order.

misuse.s: A procedure is one random action with no order and no steps.
misuse.why: A procedure is a set of steps in a fixed order, not one random action.

visual.alt: A clipboard with a checklist and check marks.

words.frame: The procedure for ___ is first ___, then ___.

words.def: Following one after another in order, with no break.
words.ex: The team won five successive games before losing in the finals.
words.ex2: Successive snowfalls on three nights left the town buried under two feet of snow.
words.nonExample: Storms scattered across different seasons are not successive.

apps.academic: Successive kings in a dynasty often continued the policies of the king before them.
apps.spoken: That was our third successive win.
apps.writing: Use successive when each item follows the last without a gap.

cloze.s: The farm lost its crop to three ___ droughts and finally closed.

cloze2.s: Winning the spelling bee in three ___ years made her a legend at the school.

misuse.s: The successive storms were scattered across different seasons with long breaks between them.
misuse.why: Successive means one right after another; long breaks between them are the opposite.

visual.alt: Three rain clouds in a row.

words.def: Easy to reach, enter, use, or understand.
words.ex: The new library has ramps and wide doors, so it is accessible to everyone.
words.ex2: The scientist explained the research in accessible language that students could follow.
words.nonExample: A cave sealed behind a locked steel door is not accessible.
words.rel: easy to get to or to understand

apps.academic: A website is accessible when people who use screen readers or keyboards can use it fully.
apps.spoken: Is the room accessible by wheelchair?
apps.writing: Use accessible for places or for writing that readers can easily reach or follow.

cloze.s: The old castle was not ___ to visitors in wheelchairs because it had only stairs.

cloze2.s: Good textbooks use clear words and pictures to make hard ideas ___ to readers.

misuse.s: The cave was accessible to everyone because it was sealed behind a locked steel door.
misuse.why: Accessible means easy to reach; a sealed, locked door makes it the opposite.

visual.alt: A wheelchair symbol beside an open doorway.

words.def: More than is needed, reasonable, or healthy.
words.ex: The coach said that running ten miles every day was excessive for a beginner.
words.ex2: Excessive noise from the construction made it hard to concentrate.
words.nonExample: Eating a reasonable lunch is not excessive.

apps.academic: Excessive use of a resource, such as water, can harm an ecosystem.
apps.spoken: That price is excessive for a plain notebook.
apps.writing: Use excessive for an amount that goes past what is reasonable, and say what the limit should be.

cloze.s: Pouring a whole bottle of syrup onto one pancake was ___, and the plate overflowed.

cloze2.s: Many residents thought the fine was ___ for such a small parking mistake, so the council voted to lower it.

misuse.s: Getting exactly the right amount of sleep is excessive, since you sleep neither too little nor too much.
misuse.why: Excessive means more than is needed; the right amount is not excessive.

visual.alt: A pancake covered by a huge pool of syrup.

passage.title: When Eastfield Threatened to Leave
paras: In the year after the factory closed, a recession settled over the town of Marlow. Shops emptied, and the floodwaters of three successive storms had barely begun to recede when the town council announced a plan to raise taxes.

The neighborhood of Eastfield, which paid the largest share, was furious. Its leaders called the increase excessive and warned that, if the council would not listen, Eastfield would secede and form its own town.

Mayor Okafor knew that a speech would not be enough. She asked the council to follow the town's procedure for hearing complaints: a public meeting, a written reply, and a vote. “We must proceed carefully,” she said, “because every step will be remembered.”

The night before the meeting, a retired judge named Mr. Abara offered to intercede. He spent the evening walking between the two groups, carrying one side's worries to the other. His request was simple. He asked that the hall be made accessible to everyone, with ramps, a hearing loop, and an interpreter, so that no resident could say they had been shut out.

At the meeting, the speeches that preceded the vote ran for three hours, and tempers cooled as each person was heard. In the end the council agreed to raise taxes in three small stages, and Eastfield agreed to stay. Mayor Okafor later told a reporter that a town does not stay together because no one disagrees. It stays together because people keep talking.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word “secede” most nearly means
choices: to vote for a new leader
to formally withdraw from a group
qs.why: Eastfield would form its own town, which means leaving the town of Marlow.

qs.q: Why do the Eastfield leaders call the tax increase excessive?
choices: They believe it is more than is fair or reasonable.
They think the town has too little money.
They want the council to stop meeting.
They think another town should pay the taxes.
qs.why: Eastfield pays the largest share and is furious, so the leaders think the increase goes past what is reasonable.

qs.q: What role does Mr. Abara play when he offers to intercede?
choices: He acts as a go-between to help the two sides understand each other.
He writes the town's new tax laws.
qs.why: He walks between the two groups carrying each side's worries to the other, which is stepping in between.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the council followed the town's procedure?
choices: The council held a public meeting, sent a written reply, and then voted.
Eastfield leaders warned that they would leave.
qs.why: A procedure is a set of steps, and the meeting, reply, and vote are the steps the mayor names.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: A community can settle a conflict when people use fair steps and keep talking.
Recessions always make towns split apart.
Judges should lead every town council.
qs.why: The dispute ends because the council follows a procedure, someone intercedes, and everyone is heard.

write.prompt: Describe a disagreement that was settled, real or imagined. Use at least three words from this unit to show who stepped in, what steps were followed, and how the conflict receded.
write.frame: When the dispute began, ___. Someone interceded by ___. We followed the procedure of ___, and the tension began to recede.

parts.m: go, yield (also spelled cede and ceed)

study.task: Make a root map with ced/cess at the center. Add six words from the unit, each with its prefix and what the whole word means. Then explain which words are spelled -cede, which are spelled -ceed, and which use cess.

sentences: Write a sentence that uses precede to show the order of two events in your day.
Write a sentence that explains why a group might secede from a larger group.
Write a sentence that uses both procedure and proceed.
Write a sentence that describes something excessive and says what a reasonable amount would be.

given: The river rose for three days.
Then the water began to go down.
The families went back to their homes.
combine.model: After the river rose for three days, the water began to recede, and the families returned to their homes.

given: The teacher helped them listen to each other.
combine.model: When two neighbors were arguing, a teacher interceded and helped them listen to each other.

discuss: When is it wiser to intercede in an argument, and when is it wiser to stay out of it? Use intercede.
How does a clear procedure help a group avoid conflict?
What makes a building, a website, or a book accessible? Give an example of each.
produce.explain: Explain how the roots in precede and recede show opposite directions. Use both words and name the prefix in each.

argue.prompt: Claim: Every public building should be fully accessible, even when it costs more to build. Take a side and support it with two reasons that use words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that accessible buildings ___ because ___. A cost that seems excessive may ___.

constructed.prompt: Describe what happens before, during, and after a storm. Use precede, proceed, and recede, and name the prefix in each word.
look: connects each prefix (pre-, pro-, re-) to its direction
constructed.model: Dark clouds precede a storm (pre- means before). The rain proceeds through the night, moving forward until morning (pro- means forward). Then the floodwater begins to recede, flowing back (re- means back).

constructed.prompt: A club is divided over a rule. Describe how members might secede, how a leader could intercede, and what procedure the club could follow. Use secede, intercede, and procedure.
look: shows intercede as stepping in between
constructed.model: Some members might secede and form a new club. The president could intercede by meeting with both groups. Then the club could follow a procedure: hold a meeting, list the concerns, and take a vote.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words built on the root ced/cess, practice how prefixes steer its meaning, and read a short narrative about a town in a tax dispute. The unit's habit is to split a word into prefix and root, state the direction, and test it against the sentence.

notes.va.precede.v: Pre- plus ced: to go before. Contrast with proceed on a two-column chart. Common error: spelling precede as preceed. Remind students that only three English verbs end in -ceed (proceed, exceed, succeed).
notes.va.proceed.v: Pro- plus ced: to go forward. Spelled -ceed, one of the three exceptions. Contrast with precede in a sentence pair so that students see the meaning change from before to forward.
notes.va.recede.v: Re- plus ced: to go back. Works for water, sound, pain, and fear. Ask students for three things that recede and what they have in common.
notes.va.secede.v: Se- means apart or away. Secede is a formal, official withdrawal. Keep the discussion on the idea and its history; do not turn the lesson into a debate about any current group.
notes.va.intercede.v: Inter- means between. Use a role-play: two students disagree, a third interceded. Ask what the risks of interceding are.
notes.va.recession.n: Re- plus cess plus -ion: a going back of the economy. A recession is a period of decline, not a single bad day. Link to the figurative sense of going back in business.
notes.va.procedure.n: Pro- plus ced plus -ure. A procedure is a set of steps in a fixed order. Practice by having students write a procedure for something familiar, then trade and follow it exactly.
notes.va.successive.adj: Suc- is a form of sub-. The key idea is no gap between items. Contrast with several, which says nothing about order. The family includes succeed and success, so link to the cess/ceed spelling pattern.
notes.va.accessible.adj: Ac- toward, cess go, -ible able to be: able to be gone to. Cover both senses: easy to reach and easy to understand. Discuss accessible design with care and respect for students with disabilities.
notes.va.excessive.adj: Ex- out or beyond, cess go: going beyond. Excessive implies a limit was passed; ask what the limit is. Students may use excessive as a stronger word for big.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “Precede. I see pre- for before and ced for go. So it means to go before. In the sentence, speeches preceded the vote, so the speeches came first. Now recede: re- means back, so to go back. The floodwater began to recede, which means it moved back. The same root points in two different directions because of the prefix.”
discuss: Which ced/cess word do you think you will use most often, and why?
How does knowing one root help you guess a word you have not seen?
misconceptions: All words that end in -ceed and -cede are spelled the same way.
Precede and proceed mean the same thing.
Secede means to lose or give up.
Accessible only refers to wheelchair access.
extend: Collect more ced/cess words from other classes (concede, success, process, access, exceed) and add them to the root map with a short meaning for each.
Write a diary entry from the point of view of someone at the meeting, using at least five unit words.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Connect concession to cede and unilateral to a decision made without consent. Revisit precede, proceed, and recede two days later with a quick prefix drill, again at one week with a new narrative, and in the conflict unit when students describe a dispute that escalates or is settled.

wida.oral: Partner A says a prefix (pre-, pro-, re-, se-, inter-). Partner B names a unit word that uses it and explains how the prefix changes the meaning of ced or cess.

needsReview: Etymology and morphology claims to confirm with a linguistics-informed reviewer: ced/cess glossed as go, yield; suc- as a form of sub- meaning after or next; ac- as a form of ad-; se- as apart or away; and the spellings cede, ceed, and cess.
Fact claims: several states seceded in 1860 and 1861 (used in an example); only proceed, exceed, and succeed end in -ceed (stated in the teacher notes).
Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: separarse formalmente (secede), retroceder (recede), interceder, and the cognate flags.
Sense boundary: recession is taught as the economic sense only.
Passage is fiction (invented town and characters).
